title: Ukraine Runs Out of Patriot Interceptors as Russian Ballistic Strikes Intensify
excerpt: Kyiv's Patriot stocks are exhausted after the latest strike on its power grid, leaving ballistic missiles largely unintercepted and resupply in doubt amid a clash with Washington.
body:
• Ukraine has exhausted its stock of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, according to a source familiar with the situation cited by CNN.
  • In the most recent Russian strike, almost all ballistic missiles went unintercepted; three Kyiv power plants were hit, four people were killed and 25 injured.
  • President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned in August that Ukraine held only about one-tenth of the interceptors it urgently needed.
  • Resupply is uncertain, with global stocks strained and Washington warning it could restrict weapons purchases if Kyiv continues strikes on Russian refineries.

Ukraine has run out of interceptor missiles for its U.S.-made Patriot air defence systems, leaving its cities and energy grid exposed to Russian ballistic missile attacks, according to reporting by CNN and the New York Post. A source familiar with the shortage said almost all ballistic missiles in the latest strike were not intercepted because the interceptors were lacking.

That attack, overnight into Wednesday, hit three power plants in Kyiv and targeted energy infrastructure in Kharkiv. Four people in Kyiv were killed and 25 injured. Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted four ballistic missiles during the defence, which CNN reported suggests those may have been among the last Patriot interceptors available.

Why Patriots Matter

Patriot interceptors are among the few weapons capable of defeating a ballistic missile in flight. Russian ballistic missiles are large, fast-moving weapons, and Ukraine has no comparable domestic substitute at scale. Kyiv has matched or surpassed Russia in drone warfare, according to both reports, but drone strength does not close the ballistic missile gap.

https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2110636794899316742

The shortage is not new. Zelensky warned for months that stocks were running low, and in August he told CNN Ukraine had only a tenth of the interceptors it urgently needed, spending his days in calls with allies seeking more. It is not thought to be the first time Ukraine has fully run out during the war.

A Strained Global Stockpile

Interceptors are expensive and in short supply worldwide. Other countries have drawn down their own stocks or held them back amid the war involving Iran and fighting in the Persian Gulf region. Production takes roughly two years, the New York Post reported, although the Trump administration is working to accelerate it.

Zelensky has also sought a licence to manufacture Patriot interceptors inside Ukraine. He said last month that President Donald Trump had approved such a request, but Trump remained noncommittal and CNN reported the licence does not appear to have been finalised.

"We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine."

— Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine

Clash With Washington

The depletion coincides with a public dispute between Zelensky and Trump. Washington has pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, struck a deal to import Russian diesel that Zelensky criticised, and warned, according to CNN, that it could suspend European purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine and intelligence sharing if the refinery strikes continued. Those purchases run through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, known as PURL, which is also a channel for future Patriot shipments.

Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian refineries this week after a pause. Zelensky told the Financial Times the block on such strikes was out, linking any renewed halt to receiving more air defences. Ukraine also reported disruptions this week to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, which were partially restored by Thursday, adding pressure on its defensive operations at the same moment its missile shield emptied.

What Comes Next

Without interceptors, each new Russian ballistic salvo is more likely to reach power plants and other infrastructure as winter approaches, raising the risk to civilians and to electricity and heating supplies. European allies have announced additional support in recent days, including British long-range missiles reported by Bloomberg, but offensive weapons do not replace the specific defensive interceptors Kyiv lacks.

The immediate question is whether the United States and its allies can find transferable stocks, finalise a production licence, or speed manufacturing fast enough to rebuild a shield that, for now, Ukrainian officials say is empty.
